title: The gap is not approval. It is proof.
mainJudgement: The gap is not approval. It is proof.

deepDive.title: It was never about the model. It’s about the harness.
deepDive.dek: What the FCA and FSB's latest warnings mean for remediation capacity, control design and correlated cyber disruption.

committeeQuestion.question: For one live change, which outcomes must still be true — and what test would show us if they no longer are?
committeeQuestion.why: Mistral's parity harness makes the point simply: approval does not prove that a changed live result remains right. The other signals show how quickly a vulnerability, provider or platform can move beyond its original assurance.
committeeQuestion.evidence: The approved baseline, two or three defined outcomes, the test run before the next release, any unresolved difference, the accountable decision and dated closure evidence.

committeeQuestions.question: Which critical service relies on a supplier or platform whose failure would leave us unable to contain, recover or explain a decision?
committeeQuestions.why: The BIS consultation brings cyber resilience and third-party dependence into the same operating conversation. AWS's investigation guidance shows the incident record needed when that dependency fails.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The service map, critical suppliers, intervention and escalation authority, tested fallback, incident timeline, recovery decision record and evidence that the service was safe to resume.

committeeQuestions.question: Can we turn a customer report, vulnerability alert or data-control exception into an owned action before it becomes an external finding?
committeeQuestions.why: ASIC's misconduct data and CISA's exploited-vulnerability update both show that available signals only matter when they reach a person with authority to investigate and act.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The intake route, triage criteria, named owner, decision log, remediation or compensating control, customer or control impact, independent retest and closed-loop reporting.

judgement.title: The gap is not approval. It is proof.
judgement.editorialAngle: Proof that a live change still meets an approved baseline
judgement.distinctFromPrevious: Edition 12 asked who owns out-of-cycle work. This edition asks for an outcome test before the next release, rather than another ownership or assurance pack.
judgement.archiveCorrection: Editorial correction, 13 September 2026: clarified the Judgement as a proof-of-outcome test and aligned the Brief and featured question.
judgement.observation: Mistral began its legacy-code migration with a parity harness: a way to prove changed code still produced the right result. This week’s signals show the same weakness: vulnerabilities, providers and data platforms can move faster than the assurance around them.
judgement.executiveJudgement: Most change governance asks whether a proposal was approved. It is weaker at detecting whether the live result has drifted from its approved baseline. A firm can have policy, owner and sign-off yet not prove that a material outcome remains right.
judgement.implication: Choose one live change. Define two or three outcomes that must remain true, test them before its next release, and take any failed or unresolved difference — not a generic control pack — to the next leadership meeting.
